This is the architecture used by the repository's custom PPO pipeline, rather than the separate skrl training example bundled with BVR Sim. The policy chooses a tactical skill and its numeric parameters. SkillManager converts that choice into heading, altitude, speed and fire guidance, which BVR Sim routes through its aircraft controllers. JSBSim computes aircraft flight dynamics inside the environment. BVR Sim also maintains the opponent, sensors, missiles and engagement events. The adapter exposes flight observations and accumulated events to our training code, which builds history and applies each pilot's own reward definition. The critic supplies learning predictions; aircraft control comes from the actor's actions and fixed skill/controller implementations. Each worker advances its own simulation; pilots do not learn against one another in these experiments.
The diagram describes this repository's custom PPO pipeline. Each pilot has its own fixed reward coefficients, actor/critic parameters, optimizer and checkpoint; pilots train independently and sequentially. Seeded scenarios specify the initial duel geometry, speeds and altitudes. The environment adapter builds a two-second observation history and accumulates combat events across 0.1-second simulator steps. The actor selects a skill and parameters roughly once per second. SkillManager converts that decision to guidance; BVR Sim manages the scripted opponent, missiles and engagement events, while aircraft controllers and JSBSim advance flight dynamics. The critic estimates discounted future own reward; it does not command the aircraft. Per-pilot event rewards, observations, actions, old action log probabilities, values and termination flags form the rollout. After 75 flights, scaled rewards and critic estimates produce GAE advantages and return targets. PPO updates the actor and critic using 256-transition minibatches, an entropy term and up to ten update passes with KL stopping. This collection/update cycle repeats for 150 epochs. Batched neural work runs on the GPU; persistent CPU workers run independent simulators. Validation uses 50 fixed, separate cases at epoch 1, every fifth epoch and the final epoch; the highest own validation return selects the checkpoint. Development cases compare those selected pilots using elimination, survival, clean wins and mutual destruction; they do not select checkpoints. Tactical continuation loads each selected actor and critic, starts a fresh Adam optimizer and adds 150 epochs against the tactical scripted opponent with the same reward profile. Future final testing is reserved for unused scenarios after development choices are fixed. Historical confirmation results in the later slides remain archived evidence.
A scenario is one seeded duel. One decision transition contains the observation, selected skill and parameters, reward, value estimate, action log probability and termination information. An epoch collects 75 duels, then optimizes using minibatches of 256 decision transitions; these are different units. Training rewards are scaled by 0.01 for GAE and critic targets, while reported returns stay in original units. GAE combines rewards and value predictions into advantages; PPO uses clipped policy updates, value fitting, entropy regularization and a KL stopping rule. Validation runs periodically without gradient updates. Checkpoints maximize each pilot's own validation reward, so differing reward profiles retain separate selection criteria. Shared development cases compare selected checkpoints using common combat outcomes and do not choose the checkpoint. Those inspected cases can still influence later experimental choices, so they are not untouched tests. The simple-opponent study uses seed 7 for training, 111257 for 50 validation cases and 211307 for 100 development cases. Tactical adaptation uses separate scenario schedules and loads each parent's actor and critic with a fresh Adam optimizer; the initial parent is also a validation candidate. The tactical stage adds 150 epochs and has its own matched before/after assessments. Future final testing uses unused cases shared across the final candidates.
Rates are equal-weight means over the same ten reward profiles. All four populations share training seed 7, validation seed 111257 and development seed 211307. Elimination means a confirmed missile elimination regardless of own survival; survival means the pilot remains alive regardless of opponent outcome. Neither is a substitute for their joint clean-win outcome. The separate parameter-head trial was not retained. The inspected benchmark is development evidence, not an untouched final test.
Notebook 06 preserves the alternative evade/pursue/eliminate reward recipe. It is a separate experiment, not the reward used by the tactical population. This is not self-play: the opponent is scripted, not another member of the learning population.
CPU workers run the JSBSim aircraft and control simulation. The GPU batches policy inference and PPO updates. Pilots train independently and sequentially; simulator workers parallelise flights within a pilot. Each epoch uses fresh training seeds; fixed validation selects checkpoints.
The actor changes action probabilities; the critic learns return targets. PPO clips probability-ratio changes and includes an entropy term. Smaller loss does not automatically mean better combat. Per-skill parameter heads were a separate architecture experiment and were not retained.
These are plausible ranges chosen as hypotheses, not calibrated optimal rewards. The population is not restricted to named aggression categories. Different weights encourage different tradeoffs but do not guarantee a particular style. Own reward chooses each pilot's checkpoint. Common benchmark reward and common outcome score are distinct summaries. Tactical adaptation reused the exact parent reward profiles; it did not add the terminal clean-win bonus.
Lower LR changed 0.0003 to 0.00003. The selected-skill correction changed action probabilities without increasing network capacity. The first intervention mainly improved survival on these cases; the second mainly increased eliminations. Overall, original to selected-skill elimination rose 12.4 points, survival 11.2 points and clean wins 21.8 points. These are observed outcome changes, not proof of a unique behavioural mechanism. Per-skill-head clean wins fell 50.0 to 42.5 percent. Bonus clean wins fell 51.5 to 49.83 percent in only six completed pilots; this subset cannot be compared directly with full-population averages.
Curves read recorded epoch metrics only. Training uses stochastic actions and changing cases; validation uses fixed cases and evaluation actions, so their returns need not coincide. Population means are descriptive: the same ten pilot reward profiles are held fixed across all four runs. Raw own reward must not rank pilots with different coefficients. Per-pilot returns and PPO losses are included in learning_curves.csv; selected-epoch validation statistics are in development_summary.csv. Historical validation files do not record the joint clean-win outcome, so it cannot be reconstructed from separate survival and elimination rates.
Tactical evades incoming missiles and supports/cranks during its own missile flight; simple pursues and fires. Both use the same JSBSim aircraft. Seeds: training 1000007 onward, validation 1100000, assessment 1120000, confirmation 1220000. Report suites never select checkpoints. Retention against simple after adaptation has not been measured.
Eliminations rose 41.8 to 48.6 percent, survival 75.1 to 83.8 and clean wins 32.7 to 38.6. Losses without elimination fell 15.8 to 6.2. Mutual destruction rose 9.1 to 10.0 and remains a tradeoff. Intervals resample shared scenarios jointly across pilots and omit training-seed variability. 005 has the highest observed confirmation clean-win rate, not a proven universal best policy. On the distinct 300-case assessment, pilot 010 leads. No pilot regressed in confirmation clean-win rate, but individual confidence intervals overlap and one tied. Selected epochs vary from 55 to 150; the final epoch is not always the saved best model.
Only eight representative skills are shown; rows therefore need not sum to 100. These are aggregate decisions, not fractions of episodes. Different exposure times and situations affect the frequencies. They support behavioural variety but do not isolate reward weights as the sole cause of style.
Own return and PPO loss are unsuitable for ranking pilots with different reward scales. The 300-case assessment improved from 31.73 to 38.67 percent, paired interval +3.87 to +9.90 points. Historical tactical and simple confirmation suites have already been inspected and cannot serve as untouched final tests in later experiments. Ongoing comparisons use recorded training, validation and fixed development cases. Final testing should occur after model and reward choices are frozen, on unused scenarios shared across all final candidates. Simulation results cannot establish real-world flight performance.
The branch also contains executed read-only report notebooks for technical follow-up. Large model weights remain in the existing local experiment directories; the presentation evidence is committed as ordinary Git files. Historical shared MP4 demonstrations depict earlier populations and must not be labelled as tactical adaptation footage.
